vignette: Ten years ago, Julian was standing in the central concourse of the regional transit terminal when the first explosion tore through the morning rush. Before the dust settled, another blast rocked the adjacent platform. Through the ringing silence came the sharp crack of gunfire and the urgent, amplified voices of law enforcement barking rapid orders through megaphones. Authorities directed passengers to press against the walls, their commands unyielding and absolute. When the situation cleared, Julian was left with a fractured sense of safety and a nervous system that had memorized the exact frequency of panic. In the months that followed, he found himself bracing for the next strike. What frightened him most was the sudden flash of aggression, whether from a startled colleague or a slammed car door. He began to avoid his regular bus route to work, turning his commute into a series of detours that ate into his mornings. He had come to believe that the world was fundamentally dangerous, that safety was a temporary illusion maintained only by constant vigilance. This conviction colored his interactions. He grew distrustful of others, convinced that people were not what they seemed, that polite exchanges could mask hidden agendas. His life, he decided, had been irreparably destroyed by the event; the man who once found joy in spontaneous dinners was gone, replaced by someone who measured every hour by potential threat. At home, his vigilance took root in the smallest details. He listened for sounds that might mean someone was entering his property, his ears tuned to settling pipes and distant trucks. Even inside his own house, he felt on guard, pacing the hallways, checking locks twice, his shoulders perpetually drawn tight. The irritability often surfaced alongside the hypervigilance. He would snap at his wife, Elena, over misplaced keys or late meals, his anger flaring without warning. These outbursts created a quiet distance. Elena began speaking in careful tones, walking softly, and Julian withdrew from shared evenings, sitting in the darkened living room rather than risk another collision. His work as a doctor became a landscape of familiar terrors. During morning rounds, senior physicians and hospital administrators spoke with the same clipped, authoritative cadence that had once echoed through the terminal. When an overhead page crackled with a directive or a department head issued an urgent order down the corridor, Julian’s pulse would spike, his breath catching as if the floor might give way. To protect himself, he began requesting fewer administrative meetings, declining committee assignments, and steering his schedule toward outpatient clinics. His colleagues noticed the withdrawal, the missed briefings, the way he avoided staff drills. The clinical fabric of his days had thinned; he was still diagnosing and prescribing, but his presence in the hospital’s institutional rhythm had faded. For three years, Julian managed through routines and restraint, but the weight of constant anticipation fractured his sleep. At sixty-three, after two decades of practice, he sat in his car one Tuesday, paralyzed by a sudden office call, and realized he could no longer trust his own mind to carry him through the day. He came to the intake hoping to quiet the noise in his head, to stop bracing for a detonation that kept coming and never coming, and to find a way back to Elena, to his patients, to the quiet certainty that his own home could once again be a place where his breathing finally slowed.
